title: Here's What's New in the iOS 27 and MacOS 27 Second Public Betas
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 23, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Cheng Xin/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple just released the second public betas of both iOS 27 and macOS 27,
                                            While the macOS 27 update seems to be mostly small improvements to performance and stability, the latest iOS 27 release did introduce some more substantive changes.
                                            Siri AI, Apple Intelligence, and Liquid Glass are the marquee features coming with the "27" software versions.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Apple just released the second public betas of both iOS 27 and macOS 27—only a week after the launch of public beta 1—so anyone signed up for the beta program can now test the latest public version of the software on their compatible iPhones and Macs. The biggest features coming to iOS 27 and macOS 27 are related to Siri AI, Apple Intelligence tools, and Liquid Glass customizations, as well as performance upgrades; so if you don't want to wait until the full release in the fall to try these out, you can install the public betas as they become available. iOS 27 and macOS 27 public beta 2 updatesLast week, Apple released iOS 27 and macOS beta 4 for developers, which 9to5Mac notes are the same build as public beta 2. While the macOS 27 update seems to be mostly bug fixes and small improvements to performance and stability, the latest developer release for iOS 27 did introduce some more substantive changes. 
For example, Siri has several additional voice options, and there's a new splash screen for Siri AI that explains its features when users open it for the first time. There's an adaptive mode slider for AirPods Pro in the Control Center, and the TV app will automatically download upcoming episodes for shows you are watching and remove downloads to manage storage space. You can also adjust how much text is previewed in chat lists, and "Zoom Photos to Fill" allows images to automatically fill your device's display. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Anyone with a compatible device can try Apple's public betas—you'll just need to enroll your Apple Account in Apple's beta program. We've covered the process for both iOS 27 and macOS 27, including which devices can run the update and the potential risks involved with installing a public beta. While public betas are typically safer than developer betas, they're not perfect, and it's always possible that bugs will slip through. At the very least, you'll want to make sure you have a backup of your data, just in case.

title: That LastPass or Bitwarden Security Email May Be a Scam
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 17, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Zooey Liao/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        You trust your password manager to keep your credentials, documents, and identity data secure—and you probably also trust notices that come from your password manager with steps to maintain that security. Scammers are counting on this: A new phishing campaign is targeting LastPass and Bitwarden users with fake security alerts designed to compromise their data and devices. Earlier this week, LastPass alerted users to an impersonation scam in which threat actors are sending phishing emails that look like official security notices. The messages come from hello[at]lastpassnewsletter[.]com with the subject line "Action Required: Review Updated LastPass Security Policies." In the email body, attackers outlined supposed changes to LastPass security monitoring and reporting protocols and noted that users "have 14 business days to review and accept the updated terms" via DocuSign. The link redirected to https[:]//lastpasscompliance[.]com/, which looked like a legitimate DocuSign page complete with a chatbot window, and prompted users to "download" DocuSign in order to review and sign the document. It's unclear whether the goal was to spread malware or harvest user credentials, as the malicious website has since been taken down. However, Bitwarden users have been targeted with a nearly identical campaign, according to BleepingComputer. 
How to spot the password manager scamOn the surface, the phishing emails targeting LastPass and Bitwarden users are pretty convincing. They have some technical jargon, so users may skim over the specifics and trust that the information is legitimate. There's a call to action, but the email states that users have 14 days to accept the terms or their account "may be temporarily restricted"—so the urgency is slightly lower than with some other scams. The email even reassures users that their vaults and accounts are "completely secure" and states that the required steps are "strictly" administrative in nature.  
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
That said, both the sender and the URL should raise suspicion. Neither lastpassnewsletter[.]com nor lastpasscompliance[.]com are official LastPass domains, nor is bitwardencompliance[.]com a real Bitwarden site. Never enter your master password or other credentials unless you navigate directly to your password manager's website or vault—links from emails, texts, or social media messages are at risk of being phishing attempts. If you've supplied your credentials to a suspicious site, update them immediately from a trusted device. You also shouldn't need to download software or use DocuSign for your password manager, and any actions on your account should occur when you are logged in to the legitimate site or vault.

title: You Can Now Verify Your Facebook Account With a Video Selfie
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

        July 24, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Facebook is adding a free verification feature that allows users to upload a selfie video and earn a white check mark.
                                            This is a separate feature from Meta Verified, which is a paid subscription for obtaining a blue check mark in Facebook and Instagram.
                                            You'll record a short selfie video, which Facebook will compare to other profile photos, but you should consider whether you want to provide more data to Meta.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're on Facebook, you may soon see a new type of verification badge on user profiles meant to indicate that there is a real, live person behind them. The platform is adding a free verification feature that allows users to upload a selfie video and earn a white check mark, which will appear on their profile and across Marketplace, Dating, and Groups. (At launch, badges won't appear in Feed posts, but Facebook says that feature will be added in the future.)Note that this is different from Meta Verified, a paid subscription that provides the blue check mark to accounts on Facebook and Instagram. This verification indicates that Meta has confirmed the user's identity based on a review of their government-issued ID and, in some cases, a selfie video. How Facebook Verified worksFacebook Verified is available to users age 18 and older whose accounts are in good standing with the platform's community standards, though the feature is launching in select markets initially before being rolled out globally. Once you have access, you'll need to record a short video selfie, which Facebook will compare to existing profile photos on your account using facial recognition. If your verification is approved, the white check mark will be added to your profile. Verification is not available for Pages or ProMode accounts. 
Consider your privacy firstFacebook says it will store your selfie video for "up to 30 days" after verification, which is a one-time process. It's not entirely clear what happens with that video in the meantime, and it's worth noting that Meta has relied on user data to train its AI. Meta AI (and Meta more broadly) is a terrible offender when it comes to privacy and security, so you should consider whether the tradeoff of a verification mark is worth handing over more of your data and read the privacy policy before you agree. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Google also launched a video selfie verification feature this week, though its purpose is to prove your identity should you get locked out of your account. Unlike Facebook Verified, which is meant to be a trust signal to other users, Google's selfie verification allows access to your entire Google account, bringing with it some additional security considerations.

title: Post-Quantum Encryption Could Be the Must-Have VPN Feature of the Future
body:
Quantum computers can't crack regular VPN encryption just yet, but what happens when that changes?
            
                        
    
                            
        
        
        July 15, 2026
            
            
                        Credit: René Ramos/Lifehacker/Adobe Stock
                            
    
        
        Cybersecurity experts warn that about 10-20 years from now, quantum computers will have enough processing power to decipher common cryptography techniques like RSA and ECC, an event they call "Q-Day." These encryption protocols are the current gold standard in VPN tech, but when Q-Day arrives, they’ll no longer be enough. Post-quantum encryption (or PQE), which uses complex mathematical puzzles that even quantum computers struggle with, is your VPN provider’s answer to the Q-Day threat. But while Q-Day is still years away from actualization, PQE is a VPN feature you can enable today, to protect your data against hackers who might hold on to your encrypted data until quantum computers get strong enough to decrypt it. NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Mullvad, and others let you enable PQE right away with the click of a button. But is this future-proof encryption protocol necessary or worth the investment today? I’ll explain how it works, what it protects against, and which providers offer it so you can make up your own mind. How post-quantum encryption (PQE) worksWhen you access the internet through a VPN tunnel, it basically scrambles your traffic data into unreadable code that can only be unlocked using a cipher key. That key is then securely transmitted to your device using a VPN handshake. So anyone who doesn’t have access to the encryption key, including your ISP, will not be able to interpret any useful information from your network and data usage. However, this technology only works because hackers don’t have access to hardware that can decrypt the scrambled network data without the encryption key. With quantum computing evolving as quickly as it is, security researchers estimate that it will be powerful enough to fully decipher your encrypted data without access to the actual key. Q-Day isn’t merely a distant threat. Attackers are already using “harvest now, decrypt later” (HNDL) attacks to hoard your encrypted network data so that they can decrypt it as soon as Q-Day arrives. That means they’ll suddenly gain access to years of private user data the second that quantum computers gain enough processing power through hardware improvements. That’s why in August 2024, the NIST standardized new encryption algorithms from an open competition that ran for years. Three models were found complex enough to resist attacks from quantum computers: ML-KEM (aka Kyber) for key exchange, along with ML-DSA and SLH-DSA for digital signatures.If your work involves sensitive data, if you perform a lot of high-value financial transactions, or if you are in a regulated industry with strict compliance requirements, PQE is worth looking into. While its availability is limited to certain VPN providers on specific pricing tiers only, security-conscious businesses and professionals operating in sensitive industries will find it genuinely useful, so it’s not just a gimmick. VPNs that support post-quantum encryptionA lot of companies use the phrase "quantum-safe" in their marketing terminology, but not all offer PQE as a standard VPN feature. Right now, NordVPN, ExpressVPN, and Mullvad are three mainstream providers who offer PQE as an opt-in feature on several plans. NordVPNNord rolled out PQE in its Linux VPN app in 2024, followed by Windows, Android, and Apple operating systems. It runs on the NordLynx protocol with the ML-KEM algorithm layered on top of the existing Wireguard encryption. But that also means you can’t use PQE with NordVPN if you’re using a dedicated IP, Meshnet, or the OpenVPN protocol. Because PQE is available to all NordLynx users, you don’t need a premium subscription tier or add-on to access it. All existing NordVPN customers can enable it, whether you’re on the Basic plan or Prime. Here’s how to do it if you’re already using NordVPN: On Windows: Open the NordVPN app, go to Settings > Connections. Toggle on Post-quantum encryption.On macOS: Open the app on your Mac device. Go to Settings, then navigate to the General tab and enable the Post-quantum encryption toggle. On iOS, Android, tvOS, or Android TV: Tap your profile icon. From here, you can easily find the toggle for Post-quantum encryption. On Linux: Navigate to terminal. Run this command: nordvpn set pq on. ExpressVPNEven before its NIST standardization, ExpressVPN was one of the first companies to offer the Kyber algorithm through its Lightway protocol as early as 2023. When the ML-KEM protocol was standardized, ExpressVPN upgraded its platform to adhere to the exact NIST standards with several improvements. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Interestingly, ExpressVPN has PQE enabled on every user plan by default. However, you need to be using the Lightway protocol and not a legacy alternative like OpenVPN. If you aren't sure if PQE is enabled, here’s how to check: Open the ExpressVPN app. Make sure you’re on the latest version of the app.Click on Settings. Navigate to the Protocol tab. Check if one of the following options is selected: Automatic, Lightway UDP, or Lightway TCP. If not, just choose any one of them to enable PQE. MullvadMullvad introduced a pilot version of its post-quantum encryption key exchange protocol way back in 2017, but the experimental implementation was replaced by a new version based on the Classic McEliece algorithm on top of all existing WireGuard servers. With the 2023.3 launch of its desktop app, Mullvad launched a fully stabilized PQE feature while extending support for Android and iOS.Mullvad doesn’t have a feature-based pricing tier to worry about. Every paying customer has access to this feature with no add-on purchases necessary. It should be enabled by default on desktop unless you specifically opted out of it, but a manual opt-in is necessary on smartphone apps. You can do this by following these steps:On Windows, macOS, and Linux: Go to Settings > VPN settings > WireGuard settings. Make sure that the Quantum-resistant tunnel option is switched to On. When the VPN is connected, you should see a string of green text that reads: “QUANTUM SECURE CONNECTION.” On Android and iOS: Launch the Mullvad VPN app. Go to Settings > VPN settings. Find the Quantum-resistant tunnel option, then toggle it on. Does it make sense to use PQE right now?There’s no downside to enabling post-quantum encryption if your VPN provider already supports it on your existing plan. I didn’t notice any meaningful latency or speed drops when testing the feature on NordVPN and ExpressVPN. But if you’re wondering if it’s worth switching to a different plan or provider just for PQE, the answer depends on what your typical workflow looks like. Quantum computers are still years away from being able to decrypt current security protocols like RSA and ECC, even by the most generous estimates. However, HNDL attacks are a big enough security red flag that companies or people operating in sensitive industries and dealing with confidential information should be paying attention. For regular browsing workflows, PQE may be overkill. But when dealing with financial data, accessing healthcare portals, or sending sensitive information that you can’t afford to have intercepted, quantum protection offers additional peace of mind.
            
                        
                
                    
                                            
                
                
                                            
    More by Ritoban

title: It Just Got a Lot Cheaper to Try Gemini Spark, Google's AI Agent
body:
Pranay Parab
                            
        
            Pranay Parab
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperiencePranay Parab is an independent tech journalist based in Mumbai, India. He covers tech for Lifehacker, and specializes in tutorials and in-depth features.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 24, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Google
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Gemini Spark, the AI agent built into Google Gemini, is now a lot cheaper to try out in the U.S. Previously, Gemini Spark was exclusive to the Google AI Ultra plan, which costs $100-$200 per month. The company is now bringing the agentic AI to its AI Pro plan, which costs $20 per month. (For now, this change is exclusive to the U.S.)When Gemini Spark was announced during Google I/O 2026, its features seemed potentially useful, but the barrier to entry was too high for most people. That appears to be changing now, as Google has cut the price by as much as 90%. It is not yet available on the $5/month AI Plus plan or the free tier, but that could change in the future too—though it's likely that using Gemini Spark on lower pricing tiers could mean that you hit your usage limits much faster.What is Gemini Spark?Google Gemini is a chatbot and a voice assistant that answers your questions, creates text, media, and even entire apps for you. Gemini Spark takes those capabilities to your Google account and executes actions for you.
You can think of Gemini Spark as a personal AI assistant that can look at your emails, calendar entries, photos, and other data in your Google account to perform tasks on your behalf. You can use Spark to bulk unsubscribe from mailing lists, make flight bookings, send reminder emails to clients, colleagues, or family members, book appointments, and much more. Having said all that, a Gemini Spark overview from out sister site PC Mag emphasizes that its features tend to overlap with Gemini. PC Mag called Spark the best AI agent yet, but that doesn't mean it's perfect.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Does Gemini Spark respect your privacy?To someone who is even remotely privacy-conscious, using Gemini Spark is going to sound quite invasive: You basically have to give it access to your entire computer if you want it to be able to act on your behalf. Google is aware of that, and has programmed the AI agent to ask for confirmations before performing certain actions. If you ask the agent to find birthday photos from 2017 and email them to someone, for example, Gemini Spark will show you the pictures and ask for a confirmation before actually sending the email. It applies the same logic to deleting emails, sending messages, using your saved credit cards to pay for reservations, and more.It's worth keeping in mind that AI services have created serious problems for people who use these apps without due caution. The biggest strength of Gemini is its access to all the data that’s in your Google account, but if you give it unrestricted access and the AI agent messes up a request, you could be stuck with an incorrect hotel reservation, a flight booked to a wrong country, or other serious consequences.

title: This App Can Help Detect When Someone Near You Is Wearing Meta Glasses
body:
Stephen Johnson
                            
        
            Stephen Johnson
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceStephen Johnson is a senior staff writer at Lifehacker covering pop culture and technology, including the columns “The Out-of-Touch Adults’ Guide to Kid Culture” and “What People Are Getting Wrong This Week.”
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 23, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Fair use
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Antizuck is a new app that scans local Bluetooth signals to detect nearby smart glasses and headsets.
                                            The app can only detect Meta glasses when they are powering on, charging, or actively pairing, rather than continuously while they are in use.
                                            Antizuck is currently only available for iPhone; an Android version is in the works.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        An app has launched that detects whether the people around you are using Meta and other kinds of smart glasses. Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner, available for iPhone and designed by Albert Pariente Cohen, detects nearby Bluetooth signals that match Meta glasses, Snap Spectacles, Meta Quest headsets, RayNeo smart glasses, and other devices; then, it lets you know what gadget is nearby and whether it's been detected previously. In keeping with the "privacy" focus, Antizuck doesn't require an account or email address, nor does it send any data outside of your phone. It retails for $2.99 with no subscription.What devices can the Antizuck app identify?In my testing, Antizuck successfully identified both my Meta glasses and my Quest 3 headset. It actually called out my Quest 3 (name and distance) while the headset was in sleep mode. The Meta glasses, though, weren't as easily detected. While it did find my glasses, it only "saw" them when I turned them off and on: Antizuck only detects Meta glasses that are charging, powering on, or while they're actively pairing. The app can also tell you all the other Bluetooth devices advertising around you, and it identifies what they are, if possible. Interestingly, it identified my charging Even Realities G2 smart glasses, but didn't flag them, I assume because they don't have a camera. Still, just seeing how many devices are broadcasting around you is worth the $3 price of admission. 
How useful are these glasses at spotting if someone is recording you?It's clear from the app's "glasses spotted" warning of "Someone may be recording near you" that the point is to let you know if a creep is creeping nearby, but they're only marginally useful for that purpose. They do not let you know which passersby are wearing Meta glasses. They don't show you an alert when a nearby pair of glasses starts recording or takes a picture, nor do they alert you when a nearby pair of Meta glasses is transferring media from the glasses to a phone. If someone turns on their glasses near you or charges them for three minutes or so, you'll get a ping and a record of whether that same pair of glasses has been detected by you in the past. But most people aren't charging their glasses on a street corner or in a bar. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Utility aside, the app is clearly part of the growing backlash against people using camera-forward smart glasses, whether it's New York banning them in court, or singer Lorde calling them "not sexy." I completely understand the concern people, particularly women, have about being recorded by hidden spy glasses, but it's not as one-sided an argument as it may appear at first. People with vision problems use Meta glasses to get verbal help from the AI. Birdwatchers use them to identify birds on the fly. I use my Meta glasses to categorize receipts for tax purposes, listen to Hawkwind, and occasionally take videos on bike rides. I'd rather not have strangers assume I'm a creep, or know that I'm wearing a specific brand of eyeglasses at all. Just as it's legal to take photos in public places, it's legal to scan your surroundings for Bluetooth signatures, but isn't each an invasion of privacy? Like anything, the only thing evil about a tool is how you use it.

title: It's Not Just You: YouTube's Picture-in-Picture Isn't Working
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 20, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: 5./15 WEST via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            As of Monday morning, YouTube's picture-in-picture (PiP) mode is broken for some users.
                                            YouTube has confirmed the issue, and says it is working on a fix.
                                            The issue appears to affect both iOS and Android, but is reportedly much more common on iPhone.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Picture-in-picture (PiP) is great for us multitaskers. While some prefer to pay full attention to their content, others prefer to keep videos running while attending to other tasks. I frequently have a video playing in PiP on both my iPhone and Mac, while I scan headlines, chat with friends, or take care of any to-do that only requires half my focus. While there are ways to manually trigger PiP, it's best on mobile, as most video player apps have adopted a natural method: When you play a video, you can simply leave the app, and the video continues playing in a PiP window. It's now muscle memory for me on iOS: I head to YouTube, choose a video, and swipe out of the app, knowing my video will keep running as I move to other apps on my iPhone.       YouTube PiP is broken (especially on iOS)Of course, like most things, PiP is only good when it works. You might have recently tried the exact shortcut I just described, only to find that nothing actually happens. You close out of YouTube, but your video doesn't follow in a PiP window. (Though it may still continue to play in the background.) And while some of you might be Android users, I'd be willing to bet most are on iPhones. What gives? 
As reported by 9to5Google, YouTube is currently experiencing issues with PiP. This isn't something only a handful of users are dealing with. The problem is apparently so widespread, YouTube has confirmed the issue directly. In a statement on YouTube Help, a Google employee shared the following:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
"We're aware that some of you are experiencing issues with the Picture-in-Picture (PiP) feature failing to trigger when exiting the YouTube app. While the vast majority of these reports are coming from iOS users, we are also seeing a significantly lower volume of reports from Android users...Our teams are actively investigating the issue, and we'll update this thread as soon as we have more information." At the time of writing, over 11,600 users hit the "I have the same question" button on this YouTube Help post. Is there any way to fix PiP in the YouTube app?Unfortunately, it doesn't seem like there is any workaround. For what it's worth, PiP was intermittent for me this morning in the YouTube app on iOS. I had no problem swiping out of a video into PiP mode during an ad, but once the video started playing, PiP didn't work. Not only that, but playback stopped as well. I went back to YouTube, played the video again, and when I left the app this time, PiP kicked in. This continued on and off, not working one time, but working the next.

schema.headline: It's Not Just You: YouTube's Picture-in-Picture Isn't Working

                                            Samsung's July Galaxy Unpacked event is set to kick off on Wednesday, July 22.
                                            The company will likely announce its next generation foldable devices, including the Galaxy Z Flip 8, Z Fold 8, and Z Fold 8 Ultra.
                                            We may also see Samsung's new smartwatches, including the Galaxy Watch 9 and Galaxy Watch Ultra 2.
                                            The event starts at 9 a.m. ET, with livestreams on both Samsung's website and YouTube channel.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        There are certain times of year we expect major tech events: Samsung hosts Galaxy Unpacked in January or February; Google hosts I/O during May; Apple's WWDC kicks off in June; and, in July, it's, um, Galaxy Unpacked...again. (I suppose that means 2026 is officially halfway through.)  While both events have the same name, Samsung's Galaxy Unpacked events are, indeed, different. February's Galaxy Unpacked, for example, unveiled the new Galaxy S26 series, including the Galaxy S26 Ultra's new Privacy Display. The company also announced its Galaxy Buds 4 and Buds 4 Pro earbuds. July's Unpacked will likely be a bit different. Here's what to expect, and how to watch:What to expect from Samsung's July 2026 Galaxy UnpackedWhere February's Unpacked was all about Samsung's flagship smartphones, July's Unpacked will likely focus on the company's foldables. As last year's foldables were the Galaxy Z 7 series (including the Galaxy Z Flip 7 and Galaxy Z Fold 7), it's likely the company will release the Galaxy Z 8 series this year, including the Galaxy Z Flip 8, the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. 
There might be more to the story than meets the eye, however. As Mashable reports, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra might be, for all intents and purposes, the Galaxy Z Fold 8—as in, the expected successor to the Galaxy Z Fold 7. The device Samsung calls the Galaxy Z Fold 8 might actually be a new device entirely, and may feature a wider display, though within a smaller frame. Samsung may also take the opportunity to roll out its next generation of smartwatches—the Galaxy Watch 9 and Galaxy Watch Ultra 2—which rumors suggest won't be changed much from the previous generation. Mashable also reports that Samsung will likely raise prices on these devices. That's no shock: As AI companies gobble up RAM and storage hardware, those goods are getting more expensive. As such, companies around the world are raising prices to protect their profits. Even Samsung itself said in April that it wouldn't be able to meet memory production demand this year, so it won't be surprising to see the company raise prices on its newest Galaxy devices. That could mean $100 increases across the board: The Fold 8 Ultra could start as high as $2,099, while the Flip 8 could cost $1,199. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Samsung isn't making it hard to watch its latest Galaxy Unpacked event. While the company is holding a limited in-person event for media, anyone with an internet connection can stream the keynote from home.Galaxy Unpacked kicks off Wednesday, July 22 at 9 a.m. ET. You can watch it on Samsung's official website or on the company's official YouTube channel.

title: MacOS 27 Comes With a Hidden Siri AI Menu
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        July 20, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NurPhoto / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple's latest macOS 27 beta comes with a hidden Siri AI menu.
                                            Once engaged, you'll see a Siri AI shortcut whenever you highlight text.
                                            You can enable the feature with a Terminal command, but it may be unstable or buggy at this time.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Siri AI is the biggest feature of Apple's upcoming suite of updates. Whether you're running iOS 27, macOS 27, or even watchOS 27, the thing that you'll likely notice first (assuming you're running a compatible device) is that Siri is much smarter now, and even more capable than it was in previous versions. If the beta previews have been any indication, this really is the biggest upgrade Apple has ever given Siri.  But it seems that the company isn't limiting itself to the upgrades it already announced. As it continues beta testing these new updates, and with them, Siri AI itself, Apple seems to be tinkering with its new AI-powered assistant, quietly planting new features that beta testers need to discover for themselves. One such feature? A new Siri AI menu that appears whenever you highlight text in macOS 27. As reported by MacRumors, this new menu appears whenever you select text in macOS 27. When you do, you'll see a floating menu in the top left of your highlighted text. If you move your cursor over it, the menu expands to reveal options, such as "Proofread," "Rewrite," "How does this sound?" and "Edit with Siri." You can also ask Siri AI to pull out key points from the text, or summarize it completely. Depending on the text, you might see other options, too: If you highlight a text from a friend, Siri AI might show you contact info; if the text contains a date, Siri AI might prompt you to create a Calendar entry. It plays into Siri AI's contextual awareness, which is part of Apple's mission to make its assistant more useful in specific scenarios. 
The thing is, this menu is disabled by default, as least as of macOS 27 developer beta 3 and public beta 1. Apple did not include it in the release notes, either; instead, a Redditor stumbled upon it, and shared instructions for turning it on on r/MacOSBeta.   Keep in mind, this feature, as with macOS 27 as a whole, is in beta testing. MacRumors says that the feature does not always work, so you may run into odd bugs or glitches after turning it on. Still, if you're already running the beta and are curious, this is an interesting feature to explore. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
To try it out, you'll need to open your Mac's Terminal app. Then, paste and run the following command: sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain && sudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/WritingTools LightweightUI_macOS -dict Enabled -bool trueYou'll need to restart your Mac for the feature to take effect. But once you do, you should see the menu whenever you highlight text—albeit with some possible hiccups. If the feature is too unstable at this point, or you simply don't like it, you can undo it by pasting the following command into Terminal: sudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/WritingTools LightweightUI_macOS -dict Enabled -bool false

David Nield
                            
        
            David Nield

            ExperienceDavid Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years. He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

        July 16, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Lifehacker
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            NotebookLM is being rebranded as Gemini Notebook.
                                            It will still work closely with the main Gemini AI app.
                                            More features are now rolling out to Google AI Pro accounts.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        NotebookLM may not be the most well-known of Google's numerous AI products, but having been introduced as Project Tailwind in May 2023, it's actually been around almost as long as the Google Gemini chatbot (originally called Bard, as you might remember).Now, perhaps in a bid to make its suite of AI tools a little less confusing, Google is renaming NotebookLM as Gemini Notebook. If you love the app in its current form, though, don't panic—not much else is changing."It remains a standalone product ... but it will now do more across the Google ecosystem, including inside the Gemini app and Google Search," explains Google. That "do more" will start with your notebooks appearing in AI Mode in Google Search for reference, which is rolling out soon.
Google's announcement post also mentions that users on the Pro plans ($19.99 a month) will soon be getting the upgrades rolled out last month, which were previously exclusive to Ultra plan users ($99.99 or $199.99 a month).These upgrades include a dedicated cloud computer for each notebook you create, enabling deeper analysis of sources and the ability to write and execute code natively (via Google Antigravity). It also means more capabilities in terms of what the app can do within each of your notebooks, including creating PDFs, charts, and slideshows, and editing them through prompts.
    
            
            The new branding for Gemini Notebook.
                                        Credit: Google
                    
    
Where Gemini ends and Gemini Notebook beginsYou could be forgiven for getting confused about the difference between the standard Gemini AI chatbot app you find on the web and mobile, and the newly renamed Gemini Notebook—especially if you've not used the latter much.They run on the same set of Gemini AI models, and can do a lot of the same tasks in terms of looking up information from the web and summarizing documents. When you've created notebooks inside Gemini Notebook, you can then also access them in the main Gemini app, confusing things even further.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
What makes Gemini Notebook different is that it's very much a research tool. You load up a bunch of sources, from YouTube videos to PDFs, and then get Gemini Notebook to query and summarize those sources, with citations.As we've written about before, you can turn your notes into audio podcasts and video overviews, as well as mind maps, flashcards, infographics and slideshows. Unlike the main Gemini app, though, it can't create images or videos out of a single prompt, without one or more sources to work from.As an addendum: If you're already a seasoned NotebookLM/Gemini Notebook user, you may have missed the latest feature upgrade, rolled out to all users a couple of weeks ago. It's called Short Video Overview, and adds a shorter, vertical video format for your summary options: Click Video Overview then Short to use it.

title: You Can Now Change the Music on Older Instagram Posts
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        July 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Instagram rolled out a new option on Tuesday that lets users change the songs on old posts.
                                            Previously, the only way to change a song on a post was to delete the post entirely and upload it again.
                                            You'll find the new feature when editing older posts, under "Original audio."
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        For frequent Instagram posters, it might seem like the app has let you add music to posts forever. But in reality, the company only rolled the feature out back in 2022. (If that doesn't sound right to you, you're just misremembering—you have been able to add music to Stories since 2018.) Over the past four years, it has been possible to attach a track to your pictures to set a mood for your post. It's a bit of an Instagram staple at this point: if you use the app with your volume up, you can't really scroll through your friends' posts without hearing a whiplash of songs.In all that time, however, adding a song was all or nothing. If you posted with a particular tune, that was the permanent soundtrack to your post. Any regrets you might have about that particular song could only be remedied by deleting the post entirely—a bit of an extreme step in most cases. As such, you might have posts in your feed with tracks you don't care for anymore, but since you don't want to take down the pictures altogether, you've had to leave them up and accept your past poor choices. But no more!Now you can change the songs on any of your Instagram posts On Tuesday, Instagram announced that songs on posts and carousels are now editable. You can swap out songs using Instagram's new "Replace Audio" feature, which lets you change the music on a post without deleting it or affecting any likes or comments. It's a simple change, but one that Instagram's user base will likely receive positively, and positive sentiment is definitely something the company needs in the wake of outcry over another high-profile feature that briefly let users generate AI images with posts from any public account. The company has since removed that option, and seems to be focused on adding new features users might actually want.    
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Changing the songs on your posts is relatively simple: Any time you want to swap out the song on one of your past posts, you can tap the two lines above the picture, tap "Edit," then choose the new "Original audio" option that appears in the menu. From here, you can change the song to anything in Instagram's library, and, presumably, return here as many times as you like to swap it out again.

title: Third-Party App Stores Are Finally Coming to Google Play
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 15, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Starting July 22, you'll be able to download third-party app marketplaces from the Play Store.
                                            The new change is the result of an agreement between Google and Epic Games.
                                            Google has strict rules for developers who distribute app stores through the Play Store.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you have an Android device, you likely download most of your apps from the Play Store. Maybe you sideload the occasional app from a website, or from your device's proprietary store (e.g., Samsung Store) but, for the most part, the Play Store is the go-to place for apps on Android. That seems to be changing. While the Play Store isn't going anywhere, Google is making third-party app stores available through its own official app store. As reported by The Verge, starting July 22, developers will be able to roll out their own app marketplaces for users to download on the Play Store. Those third-party app marketplaces can then sell their own apps, as well as pull from apps that Google hosts on the Play Store. In fact, all apps created by U.S.-based developers will be made available on these third-party app marketplaces, unless those developers opt out.While third-party app marketplaces can distribute apps outside of the Play Store, they are still subject to Google's rules. In fact, there's a host of requirements developers must follow, including terms regarding security, privacy, and user safety. In addition, app marketplace developers will need to pay Google $5,000 upfront for security and policy reviews to onboard Play Store apps, and will need to pay the fee annually.   
Why are third-party app marketplaces coming to the Play Store now?As The Verge explains, this decision is the byproduct of an agreement between Google and Epic Games. Epic Games has been taking Google and Apple to court for years, ever since Fortnite was pulled from both the iOS App Store and the Play Store. Epic Games was frustrated by both platforms' steep fees for developers, and, in protest, offered a way for users to pay Epic Games directly to skirt the fees—violating App Store and Play Store policies.   Back in 2021, a judge decreed that Google had an illegal monopoly over Android applications, and, as such, needed to allow third-party app stores to operate on its platform. Google has been trying to undo the ruling for nearly two years since, and nearly succeeded, by getting Epic Games to settle the case for $800 million. Google had agreed to allow third-party app stores, but not through its Play Store, which the judge found insufficient. Both Google and Epic Games were due in court on Thursday to continue the discussion, but Google has since withdrawn its motion. A spokesperson for the company shared the following with the judge:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
"We’ve agreed with Epic to withdraw our motion to modify the U.S. Court’s injunction rather than prolonging this process which creates uncertainty for the ecosystem. This allows us to focus on executing our recently announced global business model evolution to deliver greater app store choice, lower prices, and more opportunities for developers and users. We remain committed to maintaining Android’s industry-leading security and fostering a competitive ecosystem where every app store and developer has the freedom to compete. In parallel, we continue to comply with the U.S. Court’s injunction." We won't know exactly how things will work until these third-party app marketplaces hit the Play Store. In theory, it should be a similar experience for users, since Google has such strict requirements for app marketplace distributors. But while Epic Games is sure to roll out a third-party app marketplace, we'll have to see who else decides to take the plunge. Apple offers third-party app stores, but only in the EU, where regulations force them to.

title: iOS 26.6 Comes With Two New Features, and One Is Key for iOS 27
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Thomas Trutschel / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple's next update isn't iOS 27: it's iOS 26.6.
                                            The update comes with two features you need to know about, one of which makes it possible to use Siri AI immediately after installing iOS 27..
                                            The other sends you an alert after you've blocked too many contacts on your iPhone, though that exact limit appears unclear.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        When you think about a big iPhone update on the horizon, iOS 27 likely comes to mind. And yet, Apple is almost ready to release a totally different update: iOS 26.6. Typically, iOS updates this close to the launch of the next major version are focused on security fixes and squashing bugs, saving any major changes for the next big numbered update. And yet, while iOS 26.6 is a decidedly small update, it's still a notable one, deliveringtwo new features you should be aware of—including one that actually lays the groundwork for iOS 27.Still in betaTo be clear, iOS 26.6 isn't actually out yet. Apple seeded the "Release Candidate" (RC) to beta testers this week; this is the version of iOS 26.6 the company intends to ship to the general public. If testers find no issues with the update, we'll be getting this version of iOS 26.6 imminently. Otherwise, Apple may make some adjustments. But regardless, these below features are coming to your iPhone with the next update.
Preparing your iPhone for Siri AIiOS 26.6's first feature won't reveal itself when you install the update on your iPhone. In fact, most of us may think iOS 26.6 has no new features at all.  But the update's most important new change is key for compatible iPhones upgrading to iOS 27. As it turns out, iOS 26.6 "optimizes the Spotlight index" on your iPhone to prepare it for iOS 27. In other words, the update gets your iPhone ready for Siri AI. Apple's AI-powered assistant relies on the new search architecture in iOS 27 to run properly. As such, if you install iOS 27 without updating to iOS 26.6 first, it may take days before Siri AI can perform as expected. By preparing your iPhone with iOS 26.6 now, you'll avoid the growing pains.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Of course, that won't benefit everyone eventually upgrading to iOS 27. While the update runs on the iPhone 12 and newer devices, only the iPhone 15 Pro and newer can try Siri AI. Still, if that's you, iOS 27's new Siri will run much more smoothly coming from iOS 26.6 than from iOS 26.5.2.     iOS 26.6's other new feature is a new alert, letting you know that you've reached iOS' limit of the number of contacts you can block. It's not clear exactly how many contacts that is, but new code in the update confirms the alert is present. The alert reads: "Blocked Contacts Limit Reached: You’ve reached the maximum number of blocked contacts. To block additional callers, remove a blocked contact in Settings."The thing is, there's no documentation of what that limit actually is. In fact, anecdotal evidence suggests that the limit is user-dependent. MacRumors reports that some users receive the alert after blocking 20,000 contacts, while others only get 8,000. I've seen comments suggesting the limit is lower still, with some claiming to hit it in the 5,000s. Nonetheless, that's a lot of blocked contacts, and will likely only apply to users who receive an overwhelming number of calls and messages from unwanted sources.

title: WhatsApp Just Announced Four New Features, Including a Huge Upgrade for CarPlay and Android Auto
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 22, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            WhatsApp just announced four new features rolling out now for iOS, Android, desktop, and the web.
                                            Overhauled CarPlay and Android Auto experiences mean you can now listen to and respond to messages, and see your call history.
                                            WhatsApp also updated its PDF viewer and editor, and now lets you share Apple Music and Spotify songs directly to your Status.
                                            Finally, iPad users can create new accounts from their tablets, without needing to use a phone number.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Samsung might have just announced a bunch of new products during its July Unpacked event, but that's not stopping WhatsApp from trying to steal headlines. As Samsung was unveiling the latest Galaxy Z devices, WhatsApp announced four new features that users on both Android and iOS can take advantage of right now. Here's what's new:WhatsApp finally works as it should in CarPlay and Android AutoThe goal of CarPlay and Android Auto is to make smartphone apps safe to use while on the road. You shouldn't text and drive, but if you can hear messages and respond to them with your voice while keeping your attention where it should be, that's a win-win. Unfortunately, that wasn't really the case with WhatsApp's previous experience in the car: You could send new messages and place WhatsApp calls, but that's it, and that made WhatsApp a much more limiting experience than other car chat apps.According to WhatsApp, that's no longer the case. The latest update overhauls the experience, finally letting you listen to and respond to your messages. In addition to placing calls, you can see your call history, so you can check whether you missed a call from somebody. You can also access your list of favorite contacts, which should make it easier to start quick calls and messages to the friends and family you talk with most often.
WhatsApp gets an improved PDF experience on web and desktopWith this update, you can now open PDFs directly in WhatsApp on the web or in the desktop app without downloading them first. What's more, you can edit those PDFs after opening them, including highlighting and annotating, while remaining in the app. WhatsApp says you can view and edit these PDFs via Adobe Acrobat, putting WhatsApp in the running against other lightweight and free PDF apps on the market.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you're listening to a song you really like on Apple Music or Spotify, you can share it across many different social media apps, and that now includes WhatsApp, too. The company says you can share tracks from these music apps to your WhatsApp Status, which, presumably, will let your friends and family check out the song themselves in Apple Music or Spotify.Sign up for a WhatsApp account from your iPadIt took a while, but WhatsApp finally got an iPad app in May of 2025. Now, over a year later, WhatsApp is letting users create an account directly from WhatsApp on iPad, without needing to tie the account to a phone number. If you or someone you know uses an iPad as their main device, this should be some welcome news.

title: Scammers Are Using FaceTime to Pose As Apple Support Reps
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        July 16, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NurPhoto / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Scammers are using FaceTime to trick users into handing over sensitive information and financial data.
                                            Scammers may make their FaceTime calls look like they're coming from Apple Support to establish trust.
                                            FaceTime gives scammers the ability to request to share or control your screen, so they can remotely take over your device.
                                            Apple is now warning users about suspicious FaceTime calls.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Scam calls are nothing new. They've gotten so bad, in fact, that many of us simply refuse to answer unrecognized phone calls. But FaceTime calls are a bit different—while a phone call can come from any device that knows your number, FaceTime calls (both video and audio calls) require an Apple device to know your FaceTime contact details, which could be either your phone number or email address. In short, FaceTime feels more personal than a phone call, which is probably why many of our guards fall a bit when we get a call that way. However, that probably shouldn't be the case, if a new scam is anything to go by.Don't trust strange FaceTime calls As spotted by Malwarebytes Labs, Apple is now warning users to be skeptical of strange FaceTime calls. It comes as an update to Apple's guide on recognizing phishing schemes, which details the many ways hackers try to trick you into handing over sensitive information or financial data. That might have something to do with the uptick in scams involving FaceTime calls. These calls may come from contacts purporting to be "Apple Support," which can be indistinguishable from legitimate phone calls on the surface. In addition, some scammers text victims directly, including their contact info in the message. 
These calls may run the gamut of schemes: The scammer may say the victim has experienced credit card fraud, or an issue with their device, or an authentication request for an account. Maybe they have a refund offer for you to take advantage of, or a limited-time deal you need to claim now. Whatever the case, the situation will likely put pressure on you to act fast, reducing the chance you'll see through the act.The point of the FaceTime call may be to lure users into a false sense of security, since, as I've said, victims may be less skeptical of a FaceTime call, especially from "Apple Support." However, it may also give hackers an advantage during the scheme: After starting via a FaceTime audio call, scammers can request to switch to a video call, and have the victim share their screen. Scammers often employ the use of video calling or sharing apps to walk victims through specific steps on their device. And while many convince users to install remote control software on their devices, FaceTime lets users request to control the other caller's screen remotely. Malwarebytes says that scammers have successfully emptied bank accounts with these schemes. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
How to protect yourself from FaceTime scamsScams are everywhere these days, but that doesn't mean they're inevitable. The best defense here is to follow some simple cybersecurity best practices. That involves assuming every call (FaceTime or otherwise) from someone other than a trusted contact is suspicious—even if the call says it's from an organization like Apple. If on a call, never share private information, especially any that could be used to access your accounts or finances. And while FaceTime scams don't necessarily rely on security vulnerabilities, it's helpful to install the latest security patches to plug any known holes in your defenses.Apple even invites you to report FaceTime calls you suspect of being malicious. If you receive one, take a screenshot of the caller ID, and send that image to [email protected].
